observations: body L1-L6: «Albumasaris» (L1, L3), «Abū Ma‘shar», «Steinschneider» and «Abalachi» are letter-spaced. «extraendis» (L2) and «extrahendis» (L5), and «radii» (L5), are printed so. The dots after «verba» (L6) are five; the dash before «Eadem» measures 10.0 pt.

body L7-L12: «‘Alī ibn Riḍwān», divided between L7 and L8, «Rabban aṭ–Ṭabarī» and «Ptolemaeo» are letter-spaced; «Ibn al–Qifṭī» and «Ibn Abī Uṣaybi‘ah» (L10-L11) are not. «aṭ–Ṭabarī» and «al–Qifṭī» have long dashes (5.2 and 5.6 pt). «quos» (L8), which refers to «capita», is printed so (the neuter would be quae).

body L13-L20: the formulas are centred, as printed; the sign printed as the A and the R joined is that of right ascension. The minus signs are printed as dashes (9.7 to 10.2 pt) and set as minus signs. The temporal hours of a degree are a sixth of its semidiurnal arc, so the first formula gives the distance from the midheaven in hours of the star's own day; the rule of L17 interpolates linearly in these hours between radiation I, which it gives on the meridian (0 hours), and radiation II, which it gives with the minus sign on the horizon (6 hours).

body L21-L25: the dash before «Cum» (L22) measures 10.2 pt. In the descendant the nadir degree is on the eastern horizon, so its oblique ascension ± 60° gives the opposite point of the radiation, and 180° is added.
body L26-L34: «Ptolemaei» (L26) and «Ḥabash» are letter-spaced; «r.–v.» has a long dash (5.2 pt). «paucum» (L32) is printed so.
notes_left L1-L5: the end of note 9 begun on p. 310. The dash before «Abunasar» measures 8.0 pt; «al-hay’ah» has a hyphen (2.5 pt).
notes_left L6-L10: «Ptolemei», «Iohannes de Saxonia», divided between L8 and L9, and «Alchabitium» are letter-spaced; «94,v.-95,r.» has a hyphen (2.9 pt). Note 2 goes on in the right column (L1-L7).

notes_right L1-L7: «ff7,r.-gg2,v.» and «30,r.-32,v.» have hyphens (3.1 and 2.8 pt); a speck stands before «eum» (L2). The dash before «Si» (L4) measures 8.6 pt, and the minus sign of L5 is printed as a dash (8.3 pt). With the simple distance in degrees the hours of distance are the distance divided by a sixth of the semidiurnal arc, so the divisor 6 of L17 of the body becomes the semidiurnal arc, as printed.

notes_right L8-L10: a great circle through the north and south points of the horizon has its poles 90° from both, on the circle through the east and west points and the zenith, the prime vertical, as printed.
